disease_info: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is a trauma- and stressor-related condition that emerges within days of exposure to an event involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation, either directly, as a witness, or through learning of it occurring to a close other. It is characterized by intrusive recollections, avoidance, negative mood, dissociation, and marked arousal that last at least 3 days but less than 1 month, with clear functional impairment. Clinically, ASD often presents with sudden changes in behavior and functioning after a discrete traumatic incident, with patients describing feeling "numb," "disconnected," or constantly on edge, and struggling to resume normal routines. It is distinguished from PTSD primarily by its shorter duration and immediate temporal relationship to the trauma; persistent symptoms beyond one month suggest progression to PTSD.

narrative.personality: A competitive, curiosity-driven young man who channels anxious, perfectionistic energy into his service work and creative pursuits.
narrative.stressor: Oscar was working a busy Friday double shift at the Providence restaurant when an attempted armed robbery erupted during the late dinner rush; a masked man pulled a gun on the bartender, and in the chaos a shot was fired, shattering glass and narrowly missing a coworker Oscar had been mentoring. Oscar had always prided himself on staying calm under pressure and orchestrating the flow of the dining room, but in the days after the incident he found himself unable to walk past the restaurant entrance without his body tensing and his mind flashing back to the sound of the gunshot. He began swapping shifts to avoid evenings, then called out altogether, telling his manager he just "couldn't be in that space" anymore, and at home he stopped going to his usual street courts and favorite late-night food spots near the scene. After almost two weeks of escalating disruption to his income, creative routines, and social life, and pressure from his family who noticed how drastically he was rearranging his life to steer clear of anything related to the restaurant, he agreed to see a psychiatrist through an employee assistance referral.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t make myself go back to the restaurant or even that block since the robbery; I go out of my way to avoid anything that reminds me of it.”

narrative.personality: A methodical, health-conscious construction manager who is both detail-focused and assertive, with a strong sense of responsibility for her crews.
narrative.stressor: Jasmine was overseeing a concrete pour at a flood-zone construction site in Houston when a sudden scaffolding failure caused a partial collapse, pinning one of her longtime crew members and narrowly missing several others standing near her. She had done multiple safety walk-throughs that morning and initially stayed composed to coordinate emergency services, but the realization that someone under her supervision was critically injured on her watch hit her hard afterward. In the two weeks that followed, she forced herself back to work yet found her usual confidence shaken; routine site noises like nail guns or dropped lumber made her jerk and lose her train of thought during briefings, and she started avoiding walking under any temporary structures, delegating field checks she used to do personally. When her startled reactions and hesitancy began to unsettle her crew and she found herself dreading simple site visits despite her commitment to the project, her husband and a trusted colleague urged her to get a professional evaluation through the company’s occupational health provider.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since that collapse, every little bang or sudden noise on site makes me jump out of my skin, and it’s starting to mess with how I do my job.”

narrative.personality: A calm, routine-loving data specialist who enjoys structure, gadgets, and quiet hobbies yet can become intensely absorbed in her interests.
narrative.stressor: Yali was driving back from a weekend hike in the Bay Area when a speeding truck lost control on a wet curve, spun across the median, and slammed into the car directly in front of her, causing a multi-vehicle pileup that she narrowly avoided by swerving onto the shoulder. She had to climb out of her own car amid smoke and debris and spent nearly an hour on the roadside, helping translate for an injured Korean-speaking passenger while waiting for emergency responders to extract people from crushed vehicles. In the two weeks after the crash, her normally predictable commute and carefully maintained routines were upended as she began rearranging her schedule to avoid that freeway entirely, turning down book club and volunteer events that required driving on highways, telling friends she just "wasn't up for it." When even short local trips made her so tense that she relied on others for rides and her supervisor noticed her asking to work from home more than usual, she recognized that her life had become organized around not encountering anything that reminded her of the accident and agreed to see a psychiatrist recommended by her primary care doctor.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Since that freeway accident, I keep changing my life around just so I don’t have to drive near where it happened or even think about it.”
